messages.author: f94f7db4d63c49bd
messages.subject: Indexing in STAN
parts:
Hi,

Let's say I have a vector of groups indicators, for example jj<-c(1,2,3,NA,NA,NA,1,2,3,NA,NA,NA,1,2,3...), given to a STAN model as data, where NA means that the observation is not associated with any group. I would like to put a prior  on the coefficients associated with the groups.  Does STAN's syntax allow  me to skip  the " NA" entries, for example by writing the  following?

vector[3] beta;
beta~ normal(0,10)
for (i in 1:n){
y[i]~normal(beta[jj[i]]*x[i],sigma)
}

Rick,

messages.author: 6ad178c9bfa534b7
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Indexing in STAN
parts:
Stan doesn't have an NA type. But you can skip over entries by having separate vectors with the indices of observations that have groups, and the groups. I'm not entirely sure what you are trying to do in your model, but rewriting the model as follows will do what your original model was doing.

data {
  int jj_n;
  int jj_idx[jj_n];
  int jj_groups[jj_n];


  ...
}
parameters {
  vector[3] beta;

  ...
}
model {
  beta ~ normal(0, 10);
  for (i in 1:jj_n) {


    y[jj_idx[i]] ~ normal(beta[jj_groups[i]] * x[jj_idx[i]], sigma);
  }
  ...

}

And the input data (in R) would be

jj<-c(1,2,3,NA,NA,NA,1,2,3,NA,NA,NA,1,2,3)


jj_n <- sum(!is.na(jj))


jj_idx <- which(!is.na(jj))


jj_groups <- jj[!is.na(jj)]

messages.author: 6ad178c9bfa534b7
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Indexing in STAN
parts:
You're going to have to do something similar. There's no NA in stan or indexing, so you have to come up with ways to make the indexing easy. There are several ways of doing what you want to do. One way of doing what you want is have beta2 and beta3 be transformed parameters of length 7. For beta2 you'd set of the group you'd want to drop to 0.  Here's an example that only uses beta2.



data {
  int n_groups; // number of groups (in the example 7)


  int beta2_const_n; // number of entries in beta2 set to 0


  int beta2_const_idx[beta2_obs_n]; // indices of entries in beta2 to set to 0


  int beta2_param_n; // number of entries in beta2 that are parameters


  int beta2_param_idx[beta2_obs_n]; // indices of entries in beta2 that are parameters


  ...

}
parameters {

  vector[n_groups] beta1;

  vector[beta2_param_n] beta2_param;

  ...
}

transformed parameters {
  vector[N] p;


  vector[n_groups] beta2;


  

  for (i in 1:beta2_const_n) {

    beta2[beta2_const_idx[i]] <- 0.0;

  }
  for (i in 1:beta2_param_n) {


    beta2[beta2_param_idx[i]] <- beta2_param[i];


  }

 
  for (i in 1:N) {


    p[i] <- beta1[kk[n]] * x1[gg[n]]] + beta2[kk[n]] * x2[gg[n]];


  }

  ...
}

...


and the data you'd pass to it would be generated in R as,


n_groups <- 7
beta2_const_n <- 4
beta2_const_idx <- c(3, 6, 7)
beta2_param_n <- 3
beta2_param_idx <- c(1, 2, 4)


The above is equivalent to doing the following manually,



beta2[1] <- beta2_param[1];

beta2[2] <- beta2_param[2];
beta2[3] <- 0.0;

beta2[4] <- beta2_param[3];
beta2[5] <- 0.0;

beta2[6] <- 0.0;
beta2[7] <- 0.0;



but I presented it in a more general form that would scale to larger numbers of groups and allowing the model to be reused with different numbers of groups.  In general, I try to preprocess the data as much as possible outside of Stan, so that the model does as little data manipulation as is necessary. 



Similar ideas are discussed in the section on Missing Data in the Stan manual.  When you are dropping the coefficient for some groups, it is equivalent to constraining it to 0.
